newsitem.title: INDIA: India's BJP to block Kashmir autonomy move.
newsitem.headline: India's BJP to block Kashmir autonomy move.

text.p: India's offer of "maximum autonomy" to troubled Kashmir suffered a setback after the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) said on Wednesday that it would stall the move in parliament.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda had pledged to discuss the question of greater autonomy for the northern state of Jammu and Kashmir after local polls, currently underway, elect a new state government early next month.

Jammu and Kashmir's largest party, the National Conference, agreed to the first polls in nine years only after Deve Gowda promised more autonomy to the Himalayan state in consulation with the new government.
"We will oppose any move in parliament to give any special status to Kashmir which other states do not enjoy," BJP deputy K.L. Sharma told reporters in the state capital of Srinagar.
The BJP is contesting the polls for the first time in Kashmir, India's only Moslem majority state. It has put up some 50 candidates for the 87-seat assembly, Sharma said.

"There is a view that the BJP is anti-Moslem," he said. "The fact is that we are the only truly secular party in India... Kashmir's problems can only be solved when the BJP rules New Delhi under (former prime minister) Atal Bihari Vajpayee."

Vajpayee became prime minister briefly following India's inconclusive general elections in May and June, when the BJP emerged as the single-largest party with the support of 195 deputies in the 545-seat parliament.

Deve Gowda, leading a fractious United Front coalition, will need a two-thirds majority in the parliament to amend the constitution to accomodate former chief minister Farooq Abdullah's quest for autonomy.
Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao had promised to grant "anything short of independence" to Kashmir, but his Congress party officals say the party was divided over the issue.
The Congress has often accused Abdullah, who heads the National Conference, of being soft on separatist militants fighting Indian rule in the Himalayan region.

Congress party leader and former deputy interior minister Sibtey Razi told reporters in Srinagar this week that recent gains by Indian security forces against Moslem militants could be neutralised if the National Conference came to power.

"I fear this normalcy we have achieved could be diverted to create an even more dangerous situation," Razi said. "Post-election developments will be more important than this current phase of politics."
The BJP opposes Kashmir's special legal status, which allows only Kashmiris to buy property in the state among other privileges.
Abdullah wants to restore Kashmir's status to a pre-1952 pact with the Indian government that would make it difficult for New Delhi to sack the state government or to impose direct rule.
New Delhi dissolved the state assembly in January 1990 after forcing Abdullah to quit as chief minister. At that time, India cited growing separatist violence for the move.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have been killed since 1990, when simmering discontent against Indian rule turned into an armed revolt in the Kashmir valley.
Separatist groups oppose elections under Indian rule and say independence and not autonomy is their goal. At least 20 people have been killed in electoral violence during the campaign.
